newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan OTC stocks due for bounce but recovery frail.
newsitem.headline: Japan OTC stocks due for bounce but recovery frail.

text.p: Japan's over-the-counter (OTC) stock index is finally picking itself up off the floor after shedding nine percent in the first half of April, but market sources say they are still sceptical about any real recovery.

"The issues propping up the index now are those with high liquidity, backed by solid earnings," said a trader at a middle-sized brokerage. "Investors are placing buy orders with only fast profits in mind."

The OTC index, comprising mostly smaller, domestic firms, crawled higher for the third consecutive day on Friday, after a 15-session losing streak was broken on Wednesday by investors trawling for bargains. In early afternoon on Friday the index was up 17.05 or 1.63 percent at 1,066.02.
But the index has tumbled some 75 percent from its record high of 4,149.20 set on July 9, 1990, and analysts said a wide array of reasons was keeping the average in the doldrums.

These include the stagnant state of the overall stock market, an unclear outlook for Japan's economy and a lack of attractive new listings that could lead the market, as fast-growing publishing and software house Softbank Corp did when it made its debut nearly three years ago.

Yamaichi Research Institute forecast year-on-year average growth of 0.1 percent at best for OTC firms' parent current profits in the 1996/97 fiscal year ended March 31. Current profit is pre-tax but includes gains and losses on securities investments and other non-operating activities.

"The myth that firms which register for trade on the OTC are fast growers is starting to crumble because of the slowing economy, and this is making investors increasingly wary of the issues," said Jardine Fleming Securities analyst Etsuko Kakuta.
Requirements for registering on the OTC market are more lax than those set by other bourses, enabling smaller, newer firms to offer their shares for trade.

Conditions are likely to improve for OTC-registered firms in the fiscal year that began this month, when Yamaichi expects a 15.5 percent rise in OTC firms' profits, exceeding the 9.4 percent average increase forecast for listed companies.
But analysts said that despite the upturn, growth would vary from firm to firm and only a handful of shares was likely to be attractive to investors.

"While the index was falling, shares such as Otsuka Kagu Ltd swam against the current, powered by solid business prospects," said Masanao Kuriyama, a Yamaichi analyst. "Investors are going to want something more than a technical correction as a reason to buy shares in the coming months."

He said weakness in the index as a whole could set in after May, when many OTC-registered firms announce results for fiscal 1996/97 and forecasts for 1997/98. He said the forecasts may bring depressing news for investors.
"The Nikkei average is full of internationally competitive issues, but small retailers and service-oriented firms, both of which face tough times ahead, are plentiful in the OTC index."

A Bank of Japan survey on short-term business sentiment released in early April showed that small non-manufacturing firms were suffering most from the effects of a rise in the sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1.

With prospects for a market recovery dim, new registrations may be postponed, the Japan Securities Dealers' Association said. To cope with stagnant liquidity, the association has been mulling beginning a margin trading system and a new registration method based on book-building instead of auctions.

Under the current auction system, investors sometimes pump up the initial offer price of debutant shares, which are then hit by massive profit-taking on the first day of trade. Many shares find it hard to recover from this initial shock.
Brokers have also tried to lure investors to the market by cutting brokerage fees, made possible by recent deregulation.
But analysts say such measures are secondary to the main issue of investor disenchantment with OTC issues.

"Everyone expects OTC shares to do well to some extent, so in order for trade to flourish some outperformers need to emerge," said Okasan Economic Research Institute senior economist Akitsugu Bando. "Any earnings reports that aren't spectacular will just give investors more reasons to sell."
